questions.title: Delete duplicates, keep the row with the smallest id
questions.answer:
DELETE FROM person
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM (
    SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn
    FROM person) t
  WHERE rn > 1);

questions.title: Trap: row counts for INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL join
questions.given: A(x) = 1,1,2,NULL B(x) = 1,1,NULL join on A.x = B.x
questions.answer:
-- INNER = 4 (each 1 in A matches both 1s in B: 2 x 2)
-- LEFT = 6 (4 + unmatched 2 + unmatched NULL)
-- RIGHT = 5 (4 + unmatched NULL in B)
-- FULL = 7 (4 + 2 from A + 1 from B)
questions.note: Duplicates multiply. NULL never equals NULL, so NULLs never match. Very commonly asked.
questions.setup:
CREATE TABLE A(x INT); INSERT INTO A VALUES (1),(1),(2),(NULL);
CREATE TABLE B(x INT); INSERT INTO B VALUES (1),(1),(NULL);

                    DATE_TRUNC('month', activity_date) AS month
           FROM activity)

FROM m a
LEFT JOIN m b ON b.user_id = a.user_id
             AND b.month = a.month + INTERVAL '1' MONTH
GROUP BY a.month;

SELECT CASE WHEN id % 2 = 1 AND id = (SELECT MAX(id) FROM seat) THEN id
            WHEN id % 2 = 1 THEN id + 1
            ELSE id - 1 END AS id,
       student
FROM seat
ORDER BY id;
questions.note: Odd ids move up, even ids move down; a last odd id stays put.

questions.title: Label each node as Root, Inner or Leaf
questions.answer:
SELECT id,
  CASE WHEN parent_id IS NULL THEN 'Root'
       WHEN id IN (SELECT parent_id FROM tree WHERE parent_id IS NOT NULL) THEN
'Inner'
       ELSE 'Leaf' END AS type
FROM tree;

questions.title: Click-through rate per ad, without division errors
questions.answer:
SELECT ad_id,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN action = 'click' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN action IN ('click', 'view') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0), 2)
AS ctr
FROM ad_events
GROUP BY ad_id;
questions.note: NULLIF(x, 0) turns a zero denominator into NULL instead of an error.

             / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN action IN ('click', 'view') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0), 2)
AS ctr
FROM ad_events
GROUP BY ad_id;

questions.title: Product pairs most often bought together
questions.answer:
SELECT a.product_id AS p1, b.product_id AS p2, COUNT(*) AS times
FROM order_items a
JOIN order_items b ON a.order_id = b.order_id
                  AND a.product_id < b.product_id
GROUP BY a.product_id, b.product_id
ORDER BY times DESC
LIMIT 10;

questions.title: Upsert new and changed rows into a target (SCD Type 1)
questions.given: target(id, name, city), staging(id, name, city)
questions.answer:
MERGE INTO target t
USING staging s ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED AND (t.name <> s.name OR t.city <> s.city) THEN
  UPDATE SET name = s.name, city = s.city
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (id, name, city) VALUES (s.id, s.name, s.city);
questions.note: Deduplicate staging first — MERGE fails when two source rows match one target row. The change condition avoids rewriting unchanged rows.
questions.ref:

USING staging s ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED AND (t.name <> s.name OR t.city <> s.city) THEN
  UPDATE SET name = s.name, city = s.city
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (id, name, city) VALUES (s.id, s.name, s.city);
questions.check: SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY id

questions.title: SCD Type 2: keep history when a customer's city changes
questions.given: dim_customer(id, city, start_date, end_date, is_current), staging(id, city)
questions.answer:
-- 1. close the current row for changed customers
UPDATE dim_customer d SET end_date = CURRENT_DATE, is_current = FALSE
WHERE d.is_current
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM staging s WHERE s.id = d.id AND s.city <> d.city);
-- 2. insert a new current row for new + changed customers
INSERT INTO dim_customer (id, city, start_date, end_date, is_current)
SELECT s.id, s.city, CURRENT_DATE, NULL, TRUE
FROM staging s
LEFT JOIN dim_customer d ON d.id = s.id AND d.is_current
WHERE d.id IS NULL;
questions.note: Order matters: close first, then insert where no current row exists. Run both in one transaction.
questions.ref:

WHERE d.is_current
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM staging s WHERE s.id = d.id AND s.city <> d.city);
-- 2. insert a new current row for new + changed customers

FROM staging s
LEFT JOIN dim_customer d ON d.id = s.id AND d.is_current
WHERE d.id IS NULL;

questions.title: Incremental load: only rows changed since the last load
questions.answer:
INSERT INTO staging
SELECT *
FROM source
WHERE updated_at > (SELECT last_loaded FROM etl_watermark
                    WHERE table_name = 'source');
UPDATE etl_watermark
SET last_loaded = (SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM staging)
WHERE table_name = 'source';
questions.note: Store the watermark in a control table. Use a small overlap window plus MERGE so late-arriving rows aren't missed.

FROM source

                    WHERE table_name = 'source');

questions.title: Rows in source missing from target, and rows that changed
questions.given: src(id, name, city), tgt(id, name, city)
questions.answer:
-- missing or changed rows (full row compare)
SELECT * FROM src
EXCEPT
SELECT * FROM tgt;
-- only ids missing completely
SELECT s.id FROM src s
LEFT JOIN tgt t ON t.id = s.id
WHERE t.id IS NULL;
questions.note: EXCEPT compares every column, and treats NULLs as equal, unlike '='.
questions.ref: SELECT * FROM src EXCEPT SELECT * FROM tgt

questions.title: Reconcile row counts between source and target per load date
questions.answer:
SELECT COALESCE(s.load_date, t.load_date) AS load_date,
       s.cnt AS src_cnt, t.cnt AS tgt_cnt
FROM (SELECT load_date, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM src GROUP BY load_date) s
FULL OUTER JOIN
     (SELECT load_date, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM tgt GROUP BY load_date) t
  ON s.load_date = t.load_date
WHERE s.cnt IS DISTINCT FROM t.cnt;
questions.note: FULL JOIN catches dates present on only one side. Real reconciliation also compares SUMs of key amounts.
questions.ref:

       s.cnt AS src_cnt, t.cnt AS tgt_cnt
FROM (SELECT load_date, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM src GROUP BY load_date) s
FULL OUTER JOIN
     (SELECT load_date, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM tgt GROUP BY load_date) t
  ON s.load_date = t.load_date
WHERE s.cnt IS DISTINCT FROM t.cnt;

questions.title: Logical order of execution of a SELECT
questions.answer:
FROM / JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING
→ SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT

questions.title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
questions.answer:
DELETE → removes rows (can use WHERE), logged, slower
TRUNCATE → removes all rows fast, keeps the table structure
DROP → removes the table and its structure
questions.note: Rollback behaviour depends on the database — say that rather than guessing.

questions.title: CTE vs subquery vs temp table
questions.answer:
CTE → readable, named step inside one query
Subquery → inline, fine for small logic
Temp table → materialized once, reused across queries
questions.note: CTEs aren't always materialized — some engines recompute them each time they're referenced.

questions.title: A query got slow. How do you debug it?
questions.answer:
1. EXPLAIN / query plan: full scans, join type, spills
2. Filter early, select only needed columns
3. Partition pruning / indexes on filter and join keys
4. Check data skew and duplicate join keys
5. Replace correlated subqueries with joins or windows
questions.note: Talk through the plan first. Guessing fixes without reading the plan is the red flag they look for.
